turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Morning. Come in, sit where you like. What's brought you down?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Nothing much. The wife made the appointment. I'm fine.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): What's she picking up on?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Says I've gone flat since the redundancy. Making a meal of it, if you ask me.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): It can sit heavier than people let on. How are you sleeping?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Fine. I sleep. Well, actually, not brilliantly. It's nothing.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Give me the night without the fine.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): I just lie there for hours, some nights. Then I'm awake around four and I don't drop off again. Stupid, really.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): When did that kick in?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, since they laid me off — last winter, or the one before, I can't separate them, maybe after the clocks went back. I've no idea.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): The date can stay fuzzy. How's the energy in the daytime?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Rubbish. Knackered. That's sitting about the house, though. I'm not ill.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): What have you stopped getting any pleasure from?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Football Saturdays with my brother — haven't been in ages. Cooking as well, I used to do proper meals, now it's toast, can't see the point.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, is this radiator doing anything? It's either freezing or roasting in here.
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm alright. I'll keep the jacket on. Always do.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): That flat, can't-be-bothered feeling — most days?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Most days. Months of it. I don't make a performance out of it.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): I need to ask this gently. Any thoughts of not wanting to be here, or of hurting yourself?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Definitely not. Never crossed my mind. I'm not about to do anything daft.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thank you, that's clear. How's eating?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): I eat enough. Well, not much, actually. She says the trousers are hanging off, but I haven't been near the scales, so don't go writing a weight down.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): No number, then. Leaving fine aside, what word fits the mood?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Low. Empty. Bored of the whole lot. I don't cry, nothing like that.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any panic, or winding yourself up?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I'm not anxious. Switched off, that's all.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): And concentrating — the telly, or when your wife talks?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Telly's a blur, couldn't tell you the plot. I drift off mid-sentence. That's the bit that's newer.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you drink?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Couple of beers most nights. A bit more since the job went. No spirits. Supposed to take the edge off.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): And smoking?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Never. Filthy habit.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any regular medicines?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): The water tablet. Little white one, every morning, for my blood pressure. Don't ask me the name, it won't come.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything from the chemist for the nights?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Nytol, the blue box, one at night when I remember, maybe three times a week. I skip it if I've had the beers. Waste of money, really.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): So you're not sure you're using it the way it's meant to be used.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. I just take one if I think of it. Could be doing it all wrong.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Were you ever put on something for your mood?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Sertraline, years ago, after my dad died. I stopped it. Head went woolly. Totally different thing.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): What dose was that, if you remember?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Fifty milligrams, I think — might have been a hundred — no, fifty, I'm pretty sure. Once a day.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): You came off it yourself?
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. After a few months I felt alright, so I didn't bother you lot again.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any allergies?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Cuff on for a second. Sorry, it's cold.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Go on. It'll be normal. Always is.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hundred and thirty-eight over eighty-six. Pulse seventy-two. Nothing worrying there.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): This is a working impression, not a finished diagnosis. It looks like a depressive episode — low mood, poor sleep, loss of interest — tied up with the redundancy.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): You can call it that. I still say I'm mostly fine.
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): I don't want to start a tablet today. If things haven't shifted in four weeks, sertraline would be the one I'd consider, but come back in four weeks either way.
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): Four weeks. She'll be thrilled I showed up.

[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): Between now and then, ease off the beers on weeknights, pick a bedtime and stick to it, and skip the Nytol if you've been drinking. If thoughts of hurting yourself ever do turn up, ring the surgery the same day or call one one one, don't wait for me.

features: colloquial_drug_names: medicines referred to by colour, purpose or brand ('the water tablet', 'Crocin', 'my sugar tablets', 'the purple inhaler'); the name is recorded as said, the normalized name only if it is clear.
vague_dates: the patient cannot date things ('since Diwali or after', 'last winter, or the one before'); no invented date; a date_uncertain item.

bad.reason: Nytol, one at night maybe three times weekly for nights is stated; generic diphenhydramine not mentioned.

omissions.text: Reduced appetite is accompanied by unquantified weight loss: his wife says 'the trousers are hanging off', but he has not been weighed and no weight should be recorded.
Patient denied suicidal thoughts more strongly than just self-harm: 'No. Definitely not. Never crossed my mind. I'm not about to do anything daft.'
Past sertraline was stopped because it made his 'head woolly' (side effect/intolerance), and he stopped it himself after a few months when he felt alright without consulting the practice.
Doctor explicitly decided not to start any tablet today.
There is mild disagreement/ambivalence: doctor says it looks like a depressive episode, while patient says 'You can call it that. I still say I'm mostly fine.'
